hook.line: Some things your body does without asking you: your eyes close in a long meeting, your mouth waters at the smell of bread. Spanish says these happen to you, not that you do them.

examples.es: Se me puso la piel de gallina.
A Tomás se le quebró la voz.
Se le llenaron los ojos de lágrimas.

rule:
You already know *se me cayó* (it fell on me, not my fault). The same pattern covers the body:

*se* + *me / te / le / nos / les* + verb + the body part

The *me* says whose body it is. So you do not add *mi*: *se me cierran los ojos*, not *se me cierran mis ojos*.

The verb agrees with the body part, not with the person: *los ojos* means *cierran*, *la voz* means *quebró*.

The order never changes: *se me*, never *me se*.

It keeps you out of the blame. *Cierro los ojos* means you shut them on purpose. *Se me cierran los ojos* means you cannot help it.
smallPrint: Teachers call this an involuntary or accidental *se*, with an indirect object that marks the person affected.

options: I am closing my eyes on purpose.
My eyes are closing on me.
I am closing his eyes.

readAndPick.es: Se me puso la piel de gallina.
options: I got goosebumps.
I put a chicken on my skin.
I bought chicken skin.

readAndPick.es: A Tomás se le quebró la voz.
options: Tomás broke the voice of a friend.
Tomás lost his voice on purpose.
Tomás's voice cracked.

readAndPick.es: Se le llenaron los ojos de lágrimas.
options: Her eyes filled with tears.
I filled her eyes with tears.
She filled the eyes of a doll.
Did I make his face red?
Did your face go red?
Did you paint a red face?
Their eyes closed on them.
Our eyes closed on us.
We closed their eyes.
I put my feet to sleep on purpose.
My feet are asleep, I put them to bed.
My feet fell asleep on me.
Their eyes were closing on them.
Her eyes were closing on her.
Our eyes were closing on us.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *cierra* or *cierran* and type the whole sentence: *Se me ___ los ojos.*
yourTurn.why: *Los ojos* is plural, so the verb is *cierran*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I got goosebumps.
yourTurn.answer: Se me puso la piel de gallina.
yourTurn.why: *Se me* plus the verb, and no *mi* before the body part.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Tomás's voice cracked.
yourTurn.answer: A Tomás se le quebró la voz.
accept: Se le quebró la voz a Tomás.
yourTurn.why: *Le* stands for Tomás, and *quebró* agrees with the single *voz*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, asking a friend (tú): Did your face go red?
yourTurn.why: *Te* is you, the friend whose face it is.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: My feet fell asleep.
Make it about *her*: *Se me llenaron los ojos de lágrimas.* Say: Her eyes filled with tears.
yourTurn.answer: Se le llenaron los ojos de lágrimas.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about *us*: *Se me cerraron los ojos.* Say: Our eyes closed on us.
yourTurn.why: *Nos* replaces *me*, and the verb still follows *los ojos*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Me* already says whose eyes they are, so use *los*, not *mis*.
Almost. The verb agrees with the body part, and *los ojos* is plural.
Almost. *Se* always comes first, then *me*, *te* or *le*.

personal: Think of the last time your body gave you away, and say it with *se me…*: tired eyes, a cracked voice, a watering mouth.
